claim: Salt-inducible kinase 3 (SIK3) plays a crucial role in various aspects of metabolism.

claim: Circadian rhythms in mammals are governed by the master oscillator located in the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).

claim: Oscillation of the circadian clock is generated by the transcriptional-translational feedback loop composed of circadian clock genes and their products.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that oscillation of the circadian clock is generated by the transcriptional-translational feedback loop composed of the circadian clock genes and their products, including the transcriptional activators CLOCK and brain/muscle ARNT-like protein 1 (BMAL1), and their negative regulators PERIODs (PER1/2/3) and CHRYPTOCHROMEs (CRY1/2)(Brown et al., 2012; Takahashi, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In cells expressing the kinase-deficient SIK3 mutant K37M, PER2 protein levels were comparable with those of control cells.
source: Cells expressing the constitutive-active SIK3 mutant T163E (Katoh et al., 2006) exhibited significantly reduced PER2 protein level in HEK293T17 cells (Figure 3a) and NIH3T3 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas in cells expressing the kinase-deficient SIK3 mutant K37M (Katoh et al., 2006) PER2 protein levels were comparable with those of control cells (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kinase activity of SIK3 is required for PER2 destabilization.
source: This suggests that the kinase activity of SIK3 is required for PER2 destabilization.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the mutant data.

claim: The relative level of the up-shifted PER2 band (relative to the total of the PER2 bands) was elevated in Sik3-OX cells compared with controls.
source: Remarkably, it was observed that the relative level of the up-shifted PER2 band (relative to the total of the PER2 bands) was elevated in Sik3-OX cells compared with controls (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Protein phosphatase (λPPase) treatment reduced the up-shifted PER2 bands, which confirmed that the shifted bands were phosphorylated forms of PER2.
source: Protein phosphatase (λPPase) treatment reduced these up-shifted PER2 bands, which confirmed that the shifted bands were phosphorylated forms of PER2 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3c.

claim: PER2 levels decreased rapidly in SIK3-OX cells compared with the control cells when protein synthesis was inhibited by treatment with cycloheximide (CHX), indicating that SIK3 accelerates PER2 degradation.
source: When protein synthesis was inhibited by treatment with cycloheximide (CHX), PER2 levels decreased rapidly in SIK3-OX cells compared with the control cells, indicating that SIK3 accelerates PER2 degradation (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: All Sik3-KD cells expressing each Sik3 shRNA exhibited elevated levels of PER2 protein.
source: All Sik3-KD cells expressing each Sik3 shRNA exhibited elevated levels of PER2 protein (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a,b), and the relative levels of the up-shifted PER2 bands were significantly reduced (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 3a,b.

claim: The relative levels of the up-shifted PER2 bands were significantly reduced in Sik3-KD cells.
source: All Sik3-KD cells expressing each Sik3 shRNA exhibited elevated levels of PER2 protein (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a,b), and the relative levels of the up-shifted PER2 bands were significantly reduced (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Reduced up-shifted band of PER2 by Sik3-KD was phosphorylation-dependent band, which was confirmed by λPPase treatment of these cells.
source: Reduced up-shifted band of PER2 by Sik3-KD was phosphorylation-dependent band, which was confirmed by λPPase treatment of these cells (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3g.

claim: Degradation of PER2 protein levels in any of the Sik3-KD cells was significantly delayed, for as long as 6 hr after CHX treatment.
source: Degradation of PER2 protein levels in any of the Sik3-KD cells was significantly delayed, for as long as 6 hr after CHX treatment (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3h.

claim: SIK3 regulates PER2 abundance and stability by mediating its phosphorylation.
source: These data strongly suggest that SIK3 regulates PER2 abundance and stability by mediating its phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Expression levels of PER2 were significantly elevated in Sik3-/- fibroblasts compared with Sik3+/+ counterparts at all time points examined.
source: Expression levels of PER2 were significantly elevated in Sik3-/- fibroblasts compared with Sik3+/+ counterparts at all time points examined.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an experimental finding.

claim: Western blot analyses demonstrated increased PER2 levels in Sik3-/- liver compared with the heterozygous mice.
source: Western blot analyses demonstrated increased PER2 levels in Sik3-/- liver compared with the heterozygous mice (Figure 4b, right), which confirmed SIK3-dependent regulation of PER2 stability.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4b.

claim: The up-shifted band of PER2 was significantly increased after incubation of PER2 with SIK3 in an in vitro kinase assay.
source: The up-shifted band of PER2 was significantly increased after incubation of PER2 with SIK3, and the total amount of PER2 was reduced in a manner dependent on the amount of SIK3 added (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5a.

claim: The total amount of PER2 was reduced in a manner dependent on the amount of SIK3 added in an in vitro kinase assay.
source: The up-shifted band of PER2 was significantly increased after incubation of PER2 with SIK3, and the total amount of PER2 was reduced in a manner dependent on the amount of SIK3 added (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5a.

claim: PER2 protein level was decreased by degradation when PER2 was incubated with higher amounts of SIK3 (400 ng and 600 ng), even after purification of tagged PER2 from cell lysate.
source: PER2 protein level was decreased by degradation when PER2 was incubated with higher amounts of SIK3 (400 ng and 600 ng), even after purification of tagged PER2 from cell lysate.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the in vitro kinase assay.

claim: An in vitro phosphatase/kinase assay demonstrated that the down-shifting effect of phosphatase pre-treatment on the PER2 band was counteracted by the addition of SIK3.
source: In contrast, an in vitro phosphatase/kinase assay demonstrated that the down-shifting effect of phosphatase pre-treatment on the PER2 band was counteracted by the addition of SIK3 (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5b.

claim: When PER2 was treated with λPPase after incubation with SIK3, the up-shifted PER2 band was significantly reduced, confirming that the up-shifted band was a form of PER2 that was phosphorylated via SIK3 signaling.
source: When PER2 was treated with λPPase after incubation with SIK3, the up-shifted PER2 band was significantly reduced, confirming that the up-shifted band was a form of PER2 that was phosphorylated via SIK3 signaling (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5c.

claim: Priming phosphorylation is not needed for SIK3-dependent phosphorylation and degradation of PER2, unlike CSNK1-mediated ones.
source: These data suggest that priming phosphorylation is not needed for SIK3-dependent phosphorylation and degradation of PER2, unlike CSNK1-mediated ones.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the phosphatase/kinase assay data.

claim: CSNK1 is known to phosphorylate PER2 and induce PER2 degradation through a proteasomal pathway.
source: As mentioned above, CSNK1 is known to phosphorylate PER2 and induce PER2 degradation through a proteasomal pathway (Akashi et al., 2002; Eide et al., 2005; Meng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: CSNK1 requires an unidentified priming kinase prior to phosphorylate its substrates.
source: It has also been reported that CSNK1 requires an unidentified priming kinase prior to phosphorylate its substrates (Gallego and Virshup, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: IC261 did not affect PER2 degradation mediated by SIK3, suggesting that SIK3-dependent PER2 degradation is independent of CSNK1-mediated PER2 degradation.
source: IC261 did not affect PER2 degradation mediated by SIK3, suggesting that SIK3-dependent PER2 degradation is independent of CSNK1-mediated PER2 degradation (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5d.

claim: KD of Sik3 increased the basal level of PER2 proteins, but had no significant effect on the CSNK1-dependent phosphorylation states and degradation.
source: As shown in Figure 3e, KD of Sik3 increased the basal level of PER2 proteins, but had no significant effect on the CSNK1-dependent phosphorylation states and degradation (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5e.

claim: PER2 phosphorylation mediated by two different kinases, CSNK1 and SIK3, are independent events.
source: Collectively, these data indicated that PER2 phosphorylation mediated by two different kinases, CSNK1 and SIK3, are independent events.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: SIK3 promotes phosphorylation of PER2 and regulates the abundance of the protein by accelerating its degradation.
source: In the current study, we found that SIK3 promotes phosphorylation of PER2 and regulates the abundance of the protein by accelerating its degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: While both CSNK1d/e and SIK3-mediated phosphorylation of PER2 and promote its degradation, the underlying mechanisms appear to differ from one another.
source: Interestingly, while both CSNK1d/e and SIK3-mediated phosphorylation of PER2 and promote its degradation, the underlying mechanisms appear to differ from one another (Figure 5d and e).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Tau mutant hamsters and mice demonstrate significant phase advance and shorter periods in physiological and behavioral rhythms.
source: While Tau mutant hamsters and mice demonstrate significant phase advance and shorter periods in physiological and behavioral rhythms (Meng et al., 2008; Ralph and Menaker, 1988), Sik3-/- mice, which are loss-of-function mutants, exhibit significant phase delay and longer circadian periods as shown in the current study (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Csnk1d KO liver exhibits significantly longer period in Per2Luc rhythms.
source: It has also been reported that Csnk1d KO liver exhibits significantly longer period in Per2Luc rhythms (Etchegaray et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Both SIK3 and CSNK1 contribute to precise circadian period determination, and deficiency of either protein results in period shortening along with stabilization of PER2.
source: These data suggest that both SIK3 and CSNK1 contribute to precise circadian period determination, and that deficiency of either protein results in period shortening along with stabilization of PER2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: While CSNK1 is involved in determination of precise circadian period length and phase, SIK3 is more important for stabilization of circadian periods and phase via intercellular coupling, as well as for photic entrainment.
source: Thus, data from the current study suggest that while CSNK1 is involved in determination of precise circadian period length and phase, SIK3 is more important for stabilization of circadian periods and phase via intercellular coupling, as well as for photic entrainment (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: While the two kinases may have an overlapping role(s) with regard to phosphorylating and destabilizing PER2, SIK3 and CSNK1 contribute differentially to circadian clock regulation.
source: In other words, while the two kinases may have an overlapping role(s) with regard to phosphorylating and destabilizing PER2, SIK3 and CSNK1 contribute differentially to circadian clock regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: SIK3 is expressed in the eye.
source: For example, SIK3 is expressed in the eye (Lizcano et al., 2004) as well as in the SCN and, hence, disruption of this gene may affect the circadian light-input pathway involving the retina, which is critical for photic-entrainment.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Disruption of SIK3 may affect the circadian light-input pathway involving the retina, which is critical for photic-entrainment.
source: For example, SIK3 is expressed in the eye (Lizcano et al., 2004) as well as in the SCN and, hence, disruption of this gene may affect the circadian light-input pathway involving the retina, which is critical for photic-entrainment.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: Constitutive expression of Per2 causes arrhythmia in vitro and in vivo.
source: It has previously been shown that constitutive expression of Per2 causes arrhythmia in vitro and in vivo (Chen et al., 2009; Yamamoto et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Accumulation of PER2 protein may partly explain the aberrant rhythmicity in Sik3-/- mice.
source: This may partly explain the aberrant rhythmicity in Sik3-/- mice due to accumulation of PER2 protein.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Desynchrony among SCN cells, which has been observed in circadian rhythm mutants, may lead to insufficient light-entrainment or inconstant behavioral rhythms.
source: Desynchrony among SCN cells, which has been observed in circadian rhythm mutants (Maywood et al., 2006), may lead to insufficient light-entrainment or inconstant behavioral rhythms.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The Sik3 gene is highly conserved in evolution, from nematodes to mammals.
source: Finally, the Sik3 gene is highly conserved in evolution, from nematodes to mammals (Okamoto et al., 2004), and Sik3 deficiency results in severe phenotypes such as high lethality after birth, and metabolic and skeletal abnormalities (Sasagawa et al., 2012; Uebi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Sik3 deficiency results in severe phenotypes such as high lethality after birth, and metabolic and skeletal abnormalities.
source: Finally, the Sik3 gene is highly conserved in evolution, from nematodes to mammals (Okamoto et al., 2004), and Sik3 deficiency results in severe phenotypes such as high lethality after birth, and metabolic and skeletal abnormalities (Sasagawa et al., 2012; Uebi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: SIK3 plays an essential role in various tissues and organs.
source: These previous studies suggest that SIK3 plays an essential role in various tissues and organs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the cited studies.

claim: Behavioral and physiological abnormalities in circadian rhythms in Sik3-/- mice may be due to defects not only in the SCN, but in other parts of the brain or in other organs or tissues.
source: Considering that animal behavior is influenced by physiological states, we cannot exclude the possibility that behavioral and physiological abnormalities in circadian rhythms in Sik3-/- mice, such as those observed in the current study, are due to defects not only in the SCN, but in other parts of the brain or in other organs or tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a caveat to the interpretation of the findings.

claim: SIK3-mediated phosphorylation regulates protein stability of PER2.
source: In addition, the present study demonstrated that SIK3-mediated phosphorylation regulates protein stability of PER2; however, this does not exclude the possibility that other clock/clock-related protein(s) is also a target of SIK3.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Other clock/clock-related protein(s) may also be a target of SIK3.
source: In addition, the present study demonstrated that SIK3-mediated phosphorylation regulates protein stability of PER2; however, this does not exclude the possibility that other clock/clock-related protein(s) is also a target of SIK3.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a caveat to the interpretation of the findings.

claim: SIK1, another isoform of the SIK subfamily, is involved in photic entrainment of the master circadian clock.
source: It has been reported that SIK1, another isoform of the SIK subfamily, is involved in photic entrainment of the master circadian clock (Jagannath et al., 2013), although its involvement in the central circadian clock remains uncertain.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Light responses in behavior observed in Sik1-KD mice and Sik3-/- mice are contrary to one another: rapid vs. delayed re-entrainment, respectively.
source: Notably, while the present study demonstrated that SIK3 regulates photic-entrainment, light responses in behavior observed in Sik1-KD mice (Jagannath et al., 2013) and Sik3-/- mice are contrary to one another: rapid vs. delayed re-entrainment, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a comparison of the findings.

claim: CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 1 (CRTC1) was proposed as a target of SIK1, which contributes to light-induced phase reset.
source: In addition, CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 1 (CRTC1) was proposed as a target of SIK1, which contributes to light-induced phase reset (Jagannath et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: SIK3 contributes to the light-input pathway in addition to the circadian clock machinery in a manner that differs from SIK1, by regulating different substrates and signaling pathways.
source: Although further studies are necessary to elucidate the involvement of the two SIK isoforms in light-resetting mechanisms, the current study suggests that SIK3 contributes to the light-input pathway in addition to the circadian clock machinery in a manner that differs from SIK1, by regulating different substrates and signaling pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A splicing mutation of Sik3 (referred to as a Sleepy mutant) resulted in significant decrease in wake time caused by extended non-REM (NREM) sleep.
source: Strikingly, Funato et al. recently reported that, by large-scale forward-genetics screen in mice to seek dominant sleep abnormalities, a splicing mutation of Sik3 (referred to as a Sleepy mutant) resulted in significant decrease in wake time caused by extended non-REM (NREM) sleep (Funato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Locomotor activity rhythms in the Sleepy mutants were normal.
source: In the Sleepy mutants in which a point mutation resulting in a lack of a protein kinase A (PKA) recognition site of the SIK3 protein, the authors also described that locomotor activity rhythms in the mutants were normal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The discrepancy between the Sleepy mutant and Sik3 KO mice could be explained by a difference in introduced mutations, that is, a partial deletion in the Sleepy mutants versus null mutation in Sik3 KO mice.
source: Although the results were in contrast to our present data, the discrepancy could be explained by a difference in introduced mutations, that is, a partial deletion in the Sleepy mutants versus null mutation in our Sik3 KO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for the discrepancy.

claim: A study in Drosophila suggested effects of SIK3 homolog on coupling of different oscillator cells and with alternative period-lengthening and shortening in different cell types.
source: More recently, a study in Drosophila suggested effects of SIK3 homolog on coupling of different oscillator cells and with alternative period-lengthening and shortening in different cell types (Fujii et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The present study in mice also observed abnormality in extracellular coupling among clock cells in Sik3-knockout mice.
source: Interestingly, the present study in mice also observed abnormality in extracellular coupling among clock cells in Sik3-knockout mice (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 2.

claim: The amplitude of dPER protein rhythms in clock neurons (DN1p) was damped in Sik3-knockdown flies under constant darkness.
source: Fujii et al. described clearly that the amplitude of dPER protein rhythms in clock neurons (DN1p) was damped in Sik3-knockdown flies under constant darkness, while they did not propose a role for SIK3 in the phosphorylation and degradation of dPER.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Fujii et al. proposed HDAC4 as a target of SIK3 since HDAC4 is one of well-established targets of SIK3 in fly.
source: Instead, they proposed HDAC4 as a target of SIK3 since HDAC4 is one of well-established targets of SIK3 in fly.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: It is possible that SIK3 regulates the mammalian circadian clock by modulating activity of HDAC4 besides PER2.
source: Thus, it is possible that SIK3 regulates the mammalian circadian clock by modulating activity of HDAC4 besides PER2 or that the effect of SIK3 on PER2 degradation is mediated by some kinases or degradation proteins, which are transcriptionally regulated by HDAC4.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: The effect of SIK3 on PER2 degradation may be mediated by some kinases or degradation proteins, which are transcriptionally regulated by HDAC4.
source: Thus, it is possible that SIK3 regulates the mammalian circadian clock by modulating activity of HDAC4 besides PER2 or that the effect of SIK3 on PER2 degradation is mediated by some kinases or degradation proteins, which are transcriptionally regulated by HDAC4.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: Reduced amplitude in Per2Luc rhythms was observed in Csnk1d KO liver.
source: By contrast, unique circadian phenotypes observed in Sik3-/- mice include the following: (i) fluctuating circadian periods and phases both in vivo (Figure 1a–f) and in vitro SCN cells (Figure 2i and j), (ii) impaired light-entrainment (Figure 1d), (iii) reduced amplitude in locomotor activity rhythm (Figure 1g), and (iv) desynchrony of rhythmicity among SCN cells (Figure 2d,h, Figure 2—video 1, Figure 2—video 2), none of which have been reported in Csnk1 mutants, except that reduced amplitude in Per2Luc rhythms was observed in Csnk1d KO liver (Etchegaray et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.
